title: Forward Plan — Both Tracks Complete
markdown:
# Forward Plan — Both Tracks Complete

## The story

Earlier today we hit a cascade: a compaction-related bug got "fixed" several times, each fix introducing new side effects that became the next bug. You diagnosed the meta-pattern, we agreed on a two-track plan to stop it, you approved it, and I went autonomous.

Both tracks are now done and committed locally. Nothing has been pushed to origin — that's your call.

Here's what happened, in plain English, tied to the bigger picture.

---

## Track 1 — The governance layer

The insight that shaped this track was yours: a good tool for bug-fixing already exists (`/build`), but it shouldn't be turned into the instar-specific process, because `/build` gets used for all kinds of other work too. The right shape is a new skill that wraps `/build` and adds the instar-specific discipline around it, with infrastructure that *forces* anyone working on instar to go through it.

**What exists now:**

There's a new `/instar-dev` skill. When you use it, six phases run in order: check the architectural principle you're about to touch, plan the change, hand off to `/build` to actually make the change, produce a written side-effects review, spawn an independent reviewer for anything high-risk, and finally write a trace file that ties the artifact to the specific files you're about to commit.

The side-effects review is structured. It forces you to answer seven questions in writing before you ship: what does this over-block, what does it under-block, is it at the right level of abstraction, does it follow the signal-vs-authority principle, what does it interact with, what external surfaces does it touch, and what's the rollback cost. "No issue identified" is a valid answer — but it has to be stated explicitly. You can't just skip a question.

The signal-vs-authority principle is now a document in the instar source tree. Short version: cheap brittle checks (regex, token matching, similarity scores) produce *signals* only, never blocking decisions. A higher-level intelligent gate with full conversational context is the only thing allowed to block. This is the rule that breaks the cascade pattern at the architecture level.

**The enforcement is structural:**

A pre-commit hook on the instar repo refuses any commit to source code unless a fresh trace file exists pointing at a filled-in artifact that actually covers the staged files. A pre-push gate does the same check at the release boundary for any upgrade notes claiming a fix or feature. Bypassing via `--no-verify` is technically possible but leaves a visible trail in git history.

**It's verified working end-to-end.** The very first commit (introducing the gate itself) rode through a one-time bootstrap exception. Right after that, I tested a throwaway source edit without an artifact — the gate blocked it cleanly with a banner identifying what was missing. Everything since then has gone through the full discipline.

---

## Track 2 — The audit and reworks

With the governance layer in place, I swept instar's source looking for every decision point — every place where the code makes a block/allow/route/kill judgment about agent behavior, session lifecycle, or information flow. That inventory is now a living document in the docs directory.

About forty-five decision points total. The classification turned up something worth flagging: **instar's core infrastructure is already well-designed against this principle.** Session lifecycle owners, recovery paths, external operation gating, autonomy gates, trust management — all of them either produce signals or combine signals with intelligent authority in the right way. The compaction cascade that triggered this whole conversation was not representative of instar's overall architecture. It was concentrated in two recent additions to the outbound messaging path that had been designed the wrong way.

**The two violators — now fixed.**

Before: three independent blockers on every agent-to-user message. A regex-based junk filter, a similarity-based dedup check, and a smart tone gate. Each held its own block power. If any one of them misfired — and they misfired often — the message died without the other two ever getting a look at the decision.

After: those three are now one. The junk detector and the dedup check became pure signal producers. The smart tone gate is the only thing with block authority, and it receives the signals alongside the conversational context, making one decision with reasoning traced to an enumerated rule list (B1 through B9).

**The tone gate itself got a reliability pass.** You noticed earlier in the session that it was blocking messages citing reasons that weren't actually in its rules — inventing "exposes internal details" when its rules only cover specific literal patterns. That's drift. The new code catches it structurally: if the gate tries to block with a rule id that isn't in the enumerated set, or with no rule id at all, the gate fails open and flags the event for the over-block audit. Every decision is logged with the full signal context, so patterns become detectable instead of just frustrating.

**The two retrospective reviews** — the pre-respawn drain and the post-mistake principle in the scaffold template — both passed cleanly. Neither introduces a decision-point violation (the drain is a context-producing helper, the principle is a template edit). Both are now documented with side-effects artifacts so future audits can trace the rationale.

---

## One honest gap

The live end-to-end verification of the pre-respawn drain still requires a natural context-exhaustion event to produce the full positive-path trace. I couldn't force it during autonomous mode without either disrupting our session or spawning a throwaway and burning quota. The CompactionSentinel's structured log will capture the first real trace when it fires in the wild. This is documented in the retrospective artifact.

---

## The bigger picture

Instar's value proposition is "get the hard infrastructure right once so every agent inherits it." The failure mode we hit earlier wasn't that instar was poorly built — it was that we kept adding quick fixes to the outbound path without stepping back and asking whether they belonged there. The new governance layer and the audit together close that gap.

Every future change to instar source now has to go through the review. Every future change claiming a bug fix has to ship with evidence. Every brittle check with blocking authority gets caught at the review stage before it can land. The principle is documented, the enforcement is structural, the inventory is living. The pattern that hit us today is now harder to repeat than it is to do right.

---

## Where things stand

Four commits, all local:

1. `feat(instar-dev)` — the new skill and enforcement hooks.
2. `refactor(outbound)` — the signal-vs-authority rework of the two outbound violators plus the tone gate hardening.
3. `docs: retrospective` — retrospective review of the pre-respawn drain and post-mistake principle.
4. `docs: decision-surface inventory` — the audit output.

Nothing pushed to origin. Ready when you are.

## Next moves (your call)

- **Push when you're satisfied.** The release gate will require matching side-effects artifacts for any NEXT.md claiming a fix. We're not there yet — there's no NEXT.md for a release bump at the moment, so pushing these commits to origin just ships the infrastructure and documentation, not a versioned release.
- **Or iterate before pushing.** If anything in the implementation or the artifacts looks wrong on closer read, we can iterate.
- **Or start a Track 3.** The audit flagged one remaining item (the coherence gate specialist reviewers could drift the same way the outbound tone gate did). Not urgent but worth closing eventually.

Your move.
